Speculative decoding pairs a small draft model with a large target model: the draft generates k tokens cheaply, then the target scores them all in one forward pass, accepting or rejecting each token via a correction procedure that guarantees the output distribution exactly matches the target. The central question here is how the token-wise acceptance rate α degrades when the draft and target model were trained on different data, use different tokenizers, or have systematically different priors over vocabulary items — not just different capacities. The key concepts are the per-token acceptance probability α = min(1, p_target(x) / p_draft(x)), the geometric relationship between α and expected tokens generated per target call (roughly 1/(1−α^k)), and the notion of distributional divergence as a structured rather than random phenomenon (the draft may be systematically wrong on specific token classes). What a beginner misses is that low α isn't just "inefficiency" — it can be adversarially concentrated: if the draft confidently over-predicts a specific set of tokens (e.g., BOS-adjacent patterns, domain-specific jargon, numerical tokens) that the target rejects at high rates, the effective speedup can collapse far below the theoretical ceiling even when aggregate vocabulary overlap looks fine. The expert also worries about the cascade effect of early rejection: because speculative decoding accepts a prefix of draft tokens and rejects at the first mismatch, a single high-rejection token class that happens to appear early in most sequences can poison the entire k-token block, making the block length k itself a liability rather than an asset.

When the draft is systematically overconfident on a specific token subclass, the optimal k shrinks — but more precisely, it becomes a position-dependent function of draft entropy, because the expected tokens accepted per block is ∑{i=1}^{k} ∏{j=1}^{i} α_j, and a single low-α position early in the chain collapses the marginal value of every token beyond it. Leviathan et al. (2023) derived that the speedup wallops at roughly (1−α^k)/(1−α) · (1/c) where c is the cost ratio; if α drops to ~0.5 on positions where the draft emits, say, numerical tokens or rare domain terms, extending k beyond 3–4 yields near-zero marginal gain while still paying the draft's inference cost for those extra tokens. The practical implication is that a fixed k — as used in the original Google PaLM speculative decoding deployment and most HuggingFace implementations — is implicitly calibrated to the average α, which means it's simultaneously too long when the draft hits bad token classes and potentially too short when it's in a fluent, on-distribution region. Systems like Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) partially address this through tree-structured drafts with variable acceptance paths, effectively letting the accepted length adapt to local draft quality rather than committing to a fixed k upfront. The deeper reason k must become entropy-dependent is that draft overconfidence is anti-correlated with the entropy signal you'd want to use as a gating criterion: a miscalibrated draft assigns low entropy (high confidence) precisely to the tokens it's most wrong about, so naively using draft entropy as a proxy for "should I extend the block?" gives you the worst possible heuristic — you extend longest exactly when you should stop soonest.

SpecTr (Sun et al., 2023) and subsequent work on "speculation confidence" show that the Euclidean distance between the draft's final hidden state and its training-time centroid for a token class is a surprisingly strong predictor of target rejection, because the draft's residual stream encodes uncertainty the softmax destroys. A second concrete signal is n-gram consistency: if the draft's proposed token breaks a high-frequency bigram or trigram pattern in the draft model's own training distribution, that inconsistency — detectable via a small auxiliary n-gram LM or even a cached frequency table — predicts rejection at rates substantially above base rate, since target models trained on cleaner or different data reject out-of-distribution local syntax at high rates. A third approach, used in draft-model-aware systems like REST (He et al., 2023), is retrieval-based: maintain a datastore of (context-hash → target-acceptance outcome) pairs from prior decoding steps, and use approximate nearest-neighbor lookup on the draft's hidden state to predict acceptance without any target computation — essentially amortizing the target's signal across similar contexts seen before. The fundamental reason any of these work is that target rejection is not uniformly distributed across token-type space; it's concentrated on systematic draft failures that leave fingerprints in the draft's own representations, so a lightweight probe trained on draft internals can recover most of the target's rejection signal at a fraction of the cost.

When the draft shifts but the rejection predictor doesn't, you get miscalibrated confidence in the predictor's own predictions — specifically, the predictor was trained on draft hidden-state geometries that no longer correspond to the new draft's internal representations, so it confidently signals "this token will be accepted" on exactly the novel token classes the shifted draft now emits with high frequency, compounding rather than correcting the overconfidence problem. The failure is structurally similar to covariate shift in any learned classifier, but it's worse here because the predictor's training signal was derived from draft-target disagreement — so when the draft shifts, both the input distribution (draft hidden states) and the implicit label distribution (which tokens the target rejects) change simultaneously, and the predictor has no mechanism to detect either change without fresh target queries. This compounds with vocabulary mismatch in a specific way: if the draft was fine-tuned on a new domain (say, code or medical text) and the target was not, the draft now proposes domain-specific tokens at higher rates, the target rejects them at high rates, but the stale predictor — trained on general-domain hidden states — maps the new domain's hidden-state geometry to "low rejection risk" because those states look superficially similar to high-confidence general-domain states it was trained on. Empirically, this is the speculative decoding analogue of the silent degradation problem documented in production ML systems: the pipeline continues to function (outputs remain target-distribution-correct, since rejection sampling is still exact), but the efficiency guarantee silently collapses — speedup ratios that were 2.5–3x can degrade to near 1x with no error signal surfacing to the operator. The practical fix requires either online recalibration of the predictor using a small sliding window of recent target scores (expensive), or deliberately making the predictor shallow enough that it generalizes poorly and thus fails loudly rather than silently — a rare case where less model capacity is the robustness-preserving choice.

The key instrumentation insight from systems like vLLM and the Hugging Face TGI codebase is that per-request metadata — block length, draft entropy histogram, first-rejection position — is essentially free to log and provides a multidimensional health signal that can be fed into an anomaly detector offline without touching the hot path. The threshold for alerting should be set relative to your SLO headroom rather than absolute acceptance rate: if your p95 latency budget tolerates α ≥ 0.7 and you're seeing a rolling 5-minute mean of 0.65, that's the trigger — not some universal "α < 0.5 is bad" rule, because the right threshold is a function of k, cost ratio c, and your specific latency contract.

The shape of the first-rejection-position distribution encodes where in the block failures concentrate, and the mean discards this entirely: a distribution with mass spiked at position 1 versus one uniformly spread across positions 1–k can produce identical means while indicating completely different failure regimes. Draft distribution shift — where the draft begins proposing tokens from a new domain — typically produces a left-shift with maintained geometric decay: rejections still fall off exponentially with position (because once the draft escapes the bad token class, subsequent tokens are fine), but the decay constant accelerates and position-1 mass increases sharply, reflecting that the new token class appears early and often. Vocabulary mismatch worsening has a different signature: it produces multimodal or position-invariant mass, because mismatched tokens appear throughout the sequence rather than clustering at sequence-initial positions — if the draft and target disagree systematically on, say, numerical tokens or subword splits, rejections scatter across all positions with roughly equal probability, flattening the geometric decay into something closer to uniform. Rejection predictor staleness has the most diagnostically distinct shape: it produces high variance with late-position spikes, because the stale predictor confidently extends blocks to positions 4–6 (suppressing early termination) where the target then rejects, so you see a paradoxical mass accumulation at high positions that a well-calibrated predictor would never allow — the tail of the distribution fattens specifically at positions beyond the predictor's historical confidence threshold. To operationalize this, fit a geometric distribution to the observed first-rejection-position histogram at calibration time, then track three statistics over time: the p(position=1) mass for draft shift, the coefficient of variation of the distribution for vocabulary mismatch (high CV indicates multimodality), and the ratio of mass beyond position k/2 to mass before it for predictor staleness — each statistic isolates one failure mode while being largely insensitive to the other two.

Position-invariant rejection holds approximately when the mismatch is tokenizer-level rather than semantic-level — specifically, when the draft and target use different subword segmentations of the same underlying text, causing systematic disagreement on boundary tokens (e.g., draft emits "ĠNew" + "york" while target would emit "ĠNew" + "York" or "ĠNewYork") that occurs with roughly equal probability wherever that surface form appears, independent of what preceded it. A second condition that enforces approximate position-independence is when the mismatch is concentrated on a high-frequency closed-class token subtype — punctuation conventions, number formatting, or whitespace tokens — whose appearance rate is roughly stationary across sequence positions; if the draft consistently uses a different apostrophe token or decimal separator than the target, rejections track that token's base rate, which is approximately context-free. The assumption breaks down badly when the mismatch is semantic and domain-specific: if the draft was trained on informal text and the target on formal text, their distributions diverge most sharply at positions following specific syntactic triggers — after "the," before a proper noun, at clause boundaries — producing highly position-conditional rejection patterns that masquerade as something other than mismatch in your distributional diagnostics. It also breaks down under prefix-dependent vocabulary activation: large target models exhibit strong contextual vocabulary narrowing, where after a domain-specific prompt prefix the target's effective distribution concentrates on a small token subset, making rejection of draft tokens highly non-stationary across positions even for the same underlying mismatch type. The practical consequence for diagnostics is that the "flat histogram = vocabulary mismatch" signature is reliable only for tokenizer-level or surface-form mismatches, but for semantic mismatches in prompted or instruction-tuned settings — which are increasingly the dominant deployment pattern — the signature degrades into something that looks locally like draft distribution shift, making the three-way diagnostic separation from the previous turn unreliable precisely in the production scenarios you care most about.

The most discriminating prompt-level property is the domain specificity score of the prompt's token distribution relative to the draft model's training prior — concretely, the KL divergence between the prompt's unigram token distribution and the draft's marginal token distribution, which you can compute cheaply using the draft's embedding layer without any forward pass through either model. If this KL is low (prompt is in-distribution for the draft) but rejection rates are high, that fingerprints semantic mismatch: the draft "understands" the prompt's surface form but its completion distribution diverges from the target's because the two models learned different response styles for the same prompt type — the canonical instruction-tuning gap. Conversely, if the KL is high (prompt tokens are rare or absent in draft training), that fingerprints draft distribution shift: the draft is operating outside its competence region entirely, producing the left-shifted geometric rejection pattern described earlier. A second complementary signal is the prompt's instruction template structure — whether it matches the draft's fine-tuning template exactly, approximately, or not at all — which is a discrete categorical feature you can detect via simple string matching against known templates (Alpaca, ChatML, Vicuna formats, etc.) and which is highly stable within a serving deployment since operators typically fix their prompt format. The actionability concern is real but manageable: within a single request batch, prompt domain and template are essentially fixed (same system prompt, same user population), so the KL-based classifier needs to be computed only once per unique system prompt prefix, cached, and reused — the instability only emerges across deployment changes (new system prompt, new user base), which are exactly the events you'd already be monitoring for operational reasons independent of speculative decoding health.
